The hypothesis claims that for a rigid family (linear subspace with fixed basis coefficients), the minimum network width N_c(w) needed to achieve zero violation (max abs error ≤ 1e-3 on holdout points) should be O(1) - constant with respect to the number of constraints w.

steps.description: Design and execute a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis about rigid vs. fat families in small feedforward networks. Steps: (1) Define the rigid family as a linear subspace (e.g., polynomial of degree d with fixed basis) and the fat family as a higher-dimensional or non-parametric family (e.g., flexible neural network with many parameters). (2) Generate w constraint samples from each family, train small feedforward networks with varying hidden widths w_range, and compute held-out max absolute error. (3) Determine N_c(w) as the minimum width achieving error ≤ 1e-3 for each w. (4) Plot N_c(w) vs. w for both families and assess scaling: rigid should show N_c(w) ~ O(1) with variance O(w^-1), fat should show non-converging heavy-tailed errors. Use symbolic_math_tool to derive theoretical scaling if needed, but rely on numerical validation.

plans.objective: [DIM: computation] The minimal width $N_c(w)$ required to achieve zero violation on $w$ constraints is bounded by the VC dimension of the network class; specifically, for a ReLU network with one hidden layer of width $h$, the VC dimension is $O(d h \log h)$ where $d$ is input dimension, so $N_c(w) \geq \Omega(w / \log w)$ to ensure solvability of the constraint system.

steps.description: To test the hypothesis on minimal width $N_c(w)$ for zero violation, I will vary the constraint system structure rather than sample size from a single function. I will generate diverse constraint systems (e.g., linear inequalities, polynomial constraints, and piecewise constraints) with increasing count $w$. For each system, I will train one-hidden-layer ReLU networks of increasing width $h$ until zero violation is achieved across all constraints. I will measure $N_c(w)$ as the minimal width achieving zero violation for each $w$, and systematically vary input dimension $d$ to test the VC dimension scaling $O(d h \log h)$. This approach directly tests the capacity bound by examining solvability across combinatorial constraint configurations, not generalization error on a single function.

plans.objective: [DIM: measure] The zero-violation probability for the rigid family converges to 1 as w increases, while the fat family remains at 0, reflecting the difference in effective degrees of freedom.

This workflow ensures precise, reproducible testing of the hypothesis with proper statistical validation.

Design and run a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that small two-layer tanh networks exhibit "rigid" solution spaces for analytic constraints. Specifically: (1) Define a family of analytic constraints (e.g., polynomial identities or differential equations) that constrain function values at w points; (2) Sweep hidden layer width N ∈ [2, 16] and constraint count w ∈ {5, 10, 20, 50}; (3) For each (w, N) pair, train a two-layer tanh network to minimize loss on w training points, then evaluate max absolute error on a held-out set of validation points; (4) Define N_c(w) as the minimal N achieving max error ≤ 1e-3 on validation points; (5) Determine rigidity: if N_c(w) is small and finite across w, the solution space is rigid; if N_c(w) exceeds scan limit or grows with w, it is "fat". Specifically, we will sweep over constraint sample sizes w (e.g., w ∈ {5, 10, 20, 50, 100}) and hidden layer widths h (e.g., h ∈ [4, 64]) to compute N_c(w) = minimum h achieving zero violation (max abs error ≤ 1e-3 on held-out constraints). We will also compute Hessian rank at solution for selected (w, h) pairs to test the low-rank subspace claim. The experiment will be run as a lightweight workflow (no heavy DFT/MD).

plans.objective: [DIM: optimization] The minimum width N_c(w) for zero violation is monotonic non-decreasing in w for the rigid family, reflecting the increasing dimension of the constraint manifold; specifically, N_c(w) ≈ ⌈log₂(w)⌉ for w up to the capacity limit. | pro: This is the most directly testable hypothesis with clear numerical predictions; it builds on the previous experiments' width scans and provides a concrete relationship to validate rigidity. con: It requires precise measurement of N_c(w) across w values, which may be sensitive to random seeds and training initialization. |

steps.description: To test the hypothesis on minimal width $N_c(w)$ for zero violation, I will vary the constraint system structure rather than sample size from a single function. I will generate diverse constraint systems by varying the number of constraints $w$ and test the minimum network width $N$ required to satisfy all constraints (zero violation). The rigid family will be defined as a set of linear constraints on a low-dimensional manifold. Specifically: (1) Define the rigid family as linear constraints on a 2D manifold parameterized by $w$ constraints; (2) For each $w \in \{4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}$, train feedforward networks with widths $N \in \{8, 16, 32, 64, 128\}$; (3) Record the minimum $N$ achieving max absolute error $\leq 10^{-3}$ on held-out constraints; (4) Verify monotonicity and log₂ scaling of $N_c(w)$, and compare against the rigid vs. fat binary criterion.
